Finding the LCM by the prime factor method
Using HCF × LCM = product
When the LCM is just the product

Prime factor method: take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either number
HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers

topics.title: HCF and LCM in daily life

learn.hook: Two temple bells ring at different speeds. When will they ring together again? The LCM knows!
points: Use the HCF when you split things into the largest equal parts or the greatest number of equal groups.
Use the LCM when you want to know when things happen together again, or the smallest amount that fits several sizes.
The HCF is never bigger than the smaller number. The LCM is never smaller than the bigger number.
If one number divides the other, the HCF is the smaller number and the LCM is the bigger number.
Check your answer by dividing: the HCF must divide both numbers, and the LCM must be divisible by both numbers.

example.q: Two bells ring every 6 minutes and every 10 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. When will they next ring together?
steps: We need the LCM of 6 and 10

learn.reallife: Bus timetables, blinking festival lights and tiling a floor with the biggest square tiles all use HCF or LCM.

games.title: HCF and LCM truths
items: The HCF of two numbers is never bigger than the smaller number.
The HCF must divide the smaller number, so it cannot be bigger.
The LCM of 4 and 6 is 24.
24 is a common multiple, but 12 is the smallest one.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers.
Example: 4 and 6 have HCF 2 and LCM 12, and 2 × 12 = 24 = 4 × 6.
If one number divides the other, their HCF is the smaller number.
Example: HCF of 5 and 20 is 5.
Two even numbers can be co-prime.
Both have the factor 2, so their HCF is at least 2.
The LCM of two numbers is a multiple of their HCF.
The HCF divides both numbers, so it divides every common multiple too.

quiz.q: Two bells ring every 6 minutes and every 10 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. When will they next ring together?
quiz.explain: LCM of 6 and 10 is 30. So they ring together again 30 minutes later, at 9:30 am.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two times (16 minutes) or uses the HCF (2 minutes)

quiz.q: A floor is 12 m long and 18 m wide. What is the side of the largest square tile (in whole metres) that covers it exactly?
quiz.explain: The tile side must divide both 12 and 18. HCF(12, 18) = 6 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM instead of the HCF

quiz.q: What is the smallest number of laddoos that can be packed completely into boxes of 6, or completely into boxes of 8?
quiz.explain: The number must be a multiple of both 6 and 8. The smallest is LCM(6, 8) = 24.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 6 × 8 without looking for a smaller common multiple

quiz.q: Arjun runs one round of the track in 4 minutes and Kabir in 6 minutes. They start together. After how many minutes will both be at the start again?
quiz.explain: We need the LCM of 4 and 6, which is 12 minutes. Arjun has done 3 rounds and Kabir 2 rounds.
quiz.mistake: Adds the times or multiplies them

quiz.q: Two traffic lights change every 40 seconds and every 60 seconds. They change together now. After how many seconds will they next change together?
quiz.mistake: Uses the HCF (20) or adds the times

quiz.q: Joseph has 30 blue and 45 green marbles. He makes the greatest number of identical groups using all of them. How many green marbles are in each group?
quiz.explain: The greatest number of groups is HCF(30, 45) = 15. Each group gets 45 ÷ 15 = 3 green marbles (and 2 blue).
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of groups instead of the green marbles in each

quiz.q: What is the smallest number bigger than 1 that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2, by 3 or by 4?
quiz.explain: LCM of 2, 3 and 4 is 12, which leaves remainder 0. Add 1: 13 leaves remainder 1 each time. (25 also works, but it is not the smallest.)
quiz.mistake: Gives the LCM and forgets to add the remainder

quiz.q: Diwali lights: red ones blink every 3 seconds, green every 5 seconds and blue every 6 seconds. They all blink together now. After how many seconds will they all blink together again?
quiz.explain: LCM of 3, 5 and 6: 3 and 6 give 6, and with 5 the LCM is 30 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies all three numbers (90) without finding the smallest common multiple

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: when should he use the HCF and when the LCM in a story problem?
teach.praise: Super! HCF for splitting into the biggest equal parts, LCM for meeting together again. Gappu is ready!
teach.nudge: Which one tells you when two things happen together again?

revise.summary: Use the HCF to split things into the largest equal parts or most equal groups, and the LCM to find when things happen together again. Check by dividing.
focus: Deciding whether a problem needs the HCF or the LCM
Bells, lights and runners meeting again (LCM)
Largest tiles or equal groups (HCF)
Checking that the HCF divides both and the LCM is divisible by both
remember: HCF → largest equal parts or greatest number of equal groups
LCM → when things happen together again, or the smallest amount that fits several sizes
HCF is never bigger than the smaller number; LCM is never smaller than the bigger number
traps: Don't add the two times or use the HCF for bells ringing together.
Don't multiply all the numbers without finding the smallest common multiple.

topics.title: HCF and LCM patterns and the ladder method

learn.hook: One ladder of divisions gives you BOTH the HCF and the LCM at once!
points: If one number divides the other (like 6 and 24), the HCF is the smaller (6) and the LCM is the larger (24).
Consecutive numbers (like 14 and 15) have HCF 1. Consecutive even numbers (like 14 and 16) have HCF 2.
Multiplying both numbers by k multiplies the HCF by k: HCF(6, 9) = 3, so HCF(12, 18) = 6.
Ladder method: divide both numbers by a common factor, write the quotients below, repeat until no common factor is left. HCF = product of the divisors; LCM = HCF × the numbers in the last row.
Shortcut: divide by a big common factor first (like 10 or 12) to finish in fewer steps.

example.q: Use the ladder method for 36 and 48.

learn.reallife: Teachers use the ladder method on the board because it finds HCF and LCM in one neat table.

quiz.q: What are the HCF and LCM of 9 and 45?
quiz.explain: 9 divides 45, so the HCF is the smaller number (9) and the LCM is the larger (45).
quiz.mistake: Swaps HCF and LCM

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 99 and 100?
quiz.explain: Consecutive numbers always have HCF 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks big numbers must share a big factor

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 46 and 48?
quiz.explain: They are consecutive even numbers, so their HCF is 2.
steps: 23 and 24 have no common factor except 1.
quiz.mistake: Applies the consecutive-number rule (HCF 1) to even numbers

quiz.q: HCF(10, 15) = 5. What is HCF(20, 30)?
quiz.explain: Both numbers were doubled, so the HCF doubles: 2 × 5 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the HCF stays the same

quiz.q: HCF(4, 6) = 2. What is HCF(400, 600)?
quiz.explain: Both numbers were multiplied by 100, so the HCF is 100 × 2 = 200.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 10 instead of 100

quiz.q: The ladder for 36 and 48 uses divisors 2, 2 and 3 and ends with 3 and 4. What is the LCM?
quiz.mistake: Gives the HCF or the product of the two numbers

quiz.q: Shortcut ladder for 60 and 84: divide both by 12 first to get 5 and 7. What is the HCF?
quiz.explain: 5 and 7 have no common factor, so the HCF is the single divisor 12.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a smaller common factor

quiz.q: Using the same shortcut ladder (÷ 12 gives 5 and 7), what is the LCM of 60 and 84?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 60 × 84 instead

teach.ask: Gappu needs the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36 before lunch. Show Gappu the ladder trick!
teach.praise: Ladder climbed! HCF 12 and LCM 72.
teach.nudge: What do you do with the numbers at the bottom of the ladder?

revise.summary: HCF and LCM follow patterns: consecutive numbers have HCF 1, and multiplying both numbers by k multiplies the HCF by k. The ladder method finds both the HCF and the LCM together.
focus: HCF and LCM when one number divides the other
HCF of consecutive numbers and consecutive even numbers
Scaling both numbers
Using the ladder method and its shortcut
remember: Consecutive numbers have HCF 1; consecutive even numbers have HCF 2
Multiplying both numbers by k multiplies the HCF by k
Ladder: HCF = product of the divisors; LCM = HCF × the numbers in the last row
traps: Don't swap the HCF and LCM: for 9 and 45, HCF 9 and LCM 45.
Don't apply the consecutive-number rule (HCF 1) to consecutive even numbers.
Don't think the HCF stays the same when both numbers are multiplied.

topics.title: The 1-to-10 number, adding fractions and Mystery Colours

learn.hook: Which is the smallest number that 1, 2, 3, ... and 10 all divide exactly? It's 2,520!
points: The smallest number divisible by every number from 1 to 10 is LCM(1, ..., 10) = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 2,520.
It needs three 2s (for 8), two 3s (for 9), one 5 and one 7.
Mahāvīrāchārya (9th century) added fractions using the LCM of the denominators: 1/4 + 1/6 → LCM 12 → 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.
Using the LCM keeps the numbers smaller than simply multiplying the denominators.
Mystery Colours: numbers are coloured by a factor rule. Study which numbers share a colour to find the rule.

example.q: Add 1/6 + 3/8 using the LCM of the denominators.

learn.reallife: A school timetable with periods of different lengths, or adding recipe amounts in fractions, uses LCMs.

topics.title: Look before you leap: leap years

learn.hook: The Earth takes about 365.2422 days to go round the Sun — that tiny 0.2422 is why we have 29 February!
points: A year (one trip of the Earth round the Sun) is about 365.2422 days, not exactly 365.
In 4 years the extra part adds up to about 4 × 0.2422 ≈ 0.97 day, so we add one day (29 February) every 4 years: a leap year has 366 days.
Rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year ...
... except century years (1900, 2100), which are leap years only if divisible by 400.
So 2000 and 2400 are leap years, but 1900 and 2100 are not.

learn.hook: 'How tall is Riya?' has one answer. 'How tall are the students in Class 7?' needs data — that's statistics!
points: Statistics means collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting and presenting data.
A statistical question expects answers that vary, so we need data: 'How long do students take to reach school?'
A non-statistical question has one fixed answer: 'What time does our school start?'
A statistical statement is a conclusion supported by data: 'Half the class walks to school.'
A representative value, like the mean or median, is one number that sums up a whole data set.

Then arrange it (organise), study it (analyse) and draw meaning (interpret).
So the order is collect, organise, analyse, interpret, present.
Answer: Collect, organise, analyse, interpret, present
quiz.mistake: Starts with drawing graphs before collecting data

quiz.q: Data for 36 students: Walk 18, Bus 9, Cycle 7, Car 2. Which statement does the data support?
options: Bus is the most common way
Half of the students walk to school
quiz.explain: 18 out of 36 is exactly half.
steps: Car (2) is the fewest, cycle is 7 (not 0), bus (9) is less than walk.

Answer: Half of the students walk to school
quiz.mistake: Reads the wrong row of the table

quiz.q: What is a representative value of a data set?
options: One number that sums up the whole data set
quiz.explain: Values like the mean and the median represent the whole data set with a single number.
steps: A representative value stands for the whole data set.
Mean and median are examples: one number for all the data.
So it is one number that sums up the whole data set.
Answer: One number that sums up the whole data set
quiz.mistake: Thinks any single value from the list will do

quiz.q: Using Walk 18, Bus 9, Cycle 7, Car 2, which statement is NOT supported by the data?

Fewer than 10 students take the bus
quiz.explain: The data shows how students travel, not what they like — and only 7 cycle.
steps: The data tells how students travel, not what they like.
Only 7 students cycle, not every student.

So 'Every student likes cycling' is NOT supported.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a claim the data says nothing about

quiz.q: Three students scored 6, 7 and 8 marks. Which is a representative value?

games.title: Mean truths
items: The mean is always one of the numbers in the data.
The mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5, which is not in the data.
Mean = sum of the values ÷ number of values.
That is how the mean is found.
If every value is increased by 2, the mean also increases by 2.
The sum grows by 2 for each value, so the mean grows by 2.
The range is the biggest value minus the smallest value.
It measures the spread of the data.
The mean of 0, 0, 0 and 12 is 12.
Sum 12 ÷ 4 values = 3.
Adding a new value equal to the mean does not change the mean.
Example: 2, 4, 6 has mean 4; 2, 4, 6, 4 also has mean 4.

topics.title: Fair shares, dot plots and zeros

learn.hook: A batter scores 0 in a match — that 0 counts! But a match washed out by rain? That's missing, not zero.
points: The mean is a fair share: if 4 friends with 3, 5, 6 and 10 laddoos share equally, each gets (3 + 5 + 6 + 10) ÷ 4 = 6.
A dot plot puts a dot above a number line for each value; tall stacks show values that repeat.
From a dot plot you can quickly see the smallest, the largest, the most common value and the spread.
Zero is a real value and must be counted. Missing data (like a match not played) is left out.
The mean and median always lie between the smallest and the largest values — never outside the range.

items: A mean can be bigger than the largest value

quiz.q: 4 friends have 3, 5, 6 and 10 laddoos. They share all of them equally. How many does each get?
quiz.explain: Total = 24, shared among 4: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. That is the mean.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total instead of the share

quiz.q: A dot plot shows the values 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5. Which value has the tallest stack of dots?

steps: The tallest stack is the value with most dots.
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest value instead of the most common

quiz.q: For the dot plot 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, what is the range?

quiz.q: A batter scores 30, 0, 45, 0 and 25 in five matches. What is the mean score?

quiz.mistake: Leaves out the zero scores

quiz.q: For the scores 30, 0, 45, 0, 25, what is the median?
quiz.explain: Sorted: 0, 0, 25, 30, 45. The middle value is 25.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle value without sorting

quiz.q: One of the matches in a series was washed out by rain. How should it be treated when finding the batter's mean?
options: Leave it out — it is missing, not a score of 0
Count it as the highest score
quiz.explain: No runs were scored because no match happened, so it is missing data.
steps: A washed-out match was never played.
The batter did not score 0; there is simply no score.
Missing data should be left out of the mean.
So leave it out — it is missing, not 0.
Answer: Leave it out — it is missing, not a score of 0
quiz.mistake: Treats missing data as zero

quiz.q: Can the mean of 4, 8 and 9 be 10?
options: No — a mean always lies between the smallest and largest values
Yes, the mean can be any number
quiz.explain: The mean is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, between 4 and 9. It can never be above 9.
steps: Answer: No — a mean always lies between the smallest and largest values
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean can lie outside the data

quiz.q: What is the median of 3, 7, 7, 12?
quiz.explain: Even count: the median is the mean of the two middle values, (7 + 7) ÷ 2 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mean (7.25) instead

learn.hook: If one billionaire walks into a tea stall, the 'average' wealth there shoots up! The median stays calm. Let's see why.
points: The median is the middle value after arranging the data from smallest to largest.
If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that appears most often. Data can have more than one mode.
One very big or very small value can pull the mean far away, but the median hardly changes.
Use the mode for 'most popular' questions, like the most common shoe size.

topics.title: Comparing groups and the story of the mean

learn.hook: About 500 years ago, 16 men lined up their left feet, toe to heel, outside a church to decide how long 'one foot' should be!
points: To compare two groups, put their dot plots side by side and compare their means and medians.
A higher mean does NOT mean every member is bigger — compare spreads too.
In 16th-century Germany, 16 men stood with their left feet toe to heel. That line was a 16-foot rod, and one-sixteenth of it was taken as one 'foot' — really the mean of the 16 feet.
Indian mathematicians had words for the mean: samīkaraṇa, 'levelling' (Mahāvīrācārya, about 850 CE) and samamiti, 'mean measure' (Bhāskarācārya, about 1150 CE). 'Sama' means equal.

learn.reallife: Doctors compare children's heights today with data from years ago to see how nutrition has changed.

topics.title: Data detective: trends, combined means and a lock puzzle

learn.hook: A lock's code is hidden behind five clues. Like a data detective, rule out digits one by one!
points: Time-series tables show values year by year. Find the change each year to estimate the next value: 120, 135, 150, 165 → about 180.
Combined mean: find each group's total, add the totals, then divide by everyone: 20 students averaging 40 and 30 averaging 50 give 2,300 ÷ 50 = 46.
The median splits sorted data into two equal halves.
Estimate vs measure: the absolute difference = how far an estimate is from the actual value, ignoring the sign. Average these to judge how good estimates are.
Data projects: decide a question, collect data (survey), organise it, summarise it and present it.

example.q: Group A: 20 students, mean 40 marks. Group B: 30 students, mean 50 marks. Find the mean of all 50 students.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers estimate next month's sales from past months' data — a time series in action.

games.title: Detective checks
items: The mean of two groups is always halfway between their means
The bigger group pulls the combined mean towards its own mean.
If an estimate is 52 s and the actual is 60 s, the absolute difference is 8 s
The median splits sorted data into two equal halves
Half the values are below it and half above.
In the clue '738: nothing is correct', 7, 3 and 8 are not in the code
So we can rule them out.
A data project starts by drawing a graph
It starts with a question to investigate.

quiz.q: A library had 120, 135, 150 and 165 visitors a day in 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. About how many might it have in 2025 if the pattern continues?
quiz.explain: The number grows by 15 each year: 165 + 15 = 180.
quiz.mistake: Repeats the last value

quiz.q: Group A: 20 students, mean 40 marks. Group B: 30 students, mean 50 marks. What is the mean for all 50 students?
quiz.mistake: Averages the two means without using group sizes

quiz.q: Why is the combined mean in that question 46 and not 45?
options: Group B has more students, so its mean counts more
Means always go up when groups join
quiz.explain: 30 students at 50 outweigh 20 students at 40, pulling the mean above 45.
steps: Group A: 20 students, mean 40 → total 800. Group B: 30 students, mean 50 → total 1500.
Group B has more students, so its mean counts more.
So the combined mean is above 45: it is 46.
Answer: Group B has more students, so its mean counts more
quiz.mistake: Thinks every group counts equally

quiz.q: Sorted heights (cm): 132, 135, 138, 140, 143, 145, 149, 151. What is the median?
quiz.explain: 8 values: the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: (140 + 143) ÷ 2 = 141.5.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mean of all values instead

quiz.q: Riya estimates one minute as 52 seconds. What is the absolute difference from the actual 60 seconds?
quiz.explain: |52 − 60| = 8 seconds. The absolute difference is never negative.
steps: Absolute difference = the gap, never negative.
So the absolute difference is 8 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Keeps a minus sign

quiz.q: Three estimates differ from the actual time by 8 s, 5 s and 2 s. What is the average difference?
quiz.mistake: Gives the total difference

quiz.q: What is the first step of a data project such as 'How long are the sentences in our textbook?'
options: Decide clearly the question to answer
quiz.explain: A clear question tells you what data to collect.
steps: A data project starts by knowing what we want to find out.
A clear question tells us what data to collect.
Graphs, means and conclusions come later.
So the first step is to decide clearly the question to answer.
Answer: Decide clearly the question to answer
quiz.mistake: Starts with the graph before collecting data

quiz.q: Lock clues: 682 — one digit right and in place; 614 — one right, wrong place; 206 — two right, wrong places; 738 — none right; 870 — one right, wrong place. What is the code?
quiz.explain: 738 rules out 7, 3 and 8. From 870 and 206, 0 is in the code but not 2nd or 3rd, so it is 1st. From 682, 2 is right and in place (3rd). From 614, 4 is in the code but not 3rd, so it is 2nd: 042.
quiz.mistake: Does not use every clue

teach.ask: Gappu's class (20 students, mean 40) joins another (30 students, mean 50). Gappu says the new mean is 45. Help!
teach.praise: Detective Gappu cracked it: the combined mean is 46!

focus: Estimating the next value from a time-series
Finding a combined mean using group sizes
Using absolute differences to judge estimates
The steps of a data project

Absolute difference = how far an estimate is from the actual value, ignoring the sign

Don't keep a minus sign in an absolute difference.
Don't start with the graph before deciding the question and collecting data.

learn.hook: Can you find the exact middle of a line without measuring? A compass can do it — like a magic trick!
points: To bisect means to cut into two equal parts.
Perpendicular bisector of AB: with a compass opening MORE than half of AB, draw arcs from A and from B on both sides. Join the two points where the arcs cross.
The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of AB and makes a 90° angle with it.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B.
Angle bisector: from the vertex draw an arc cutting both arms. From those two points draw arcs that cross. Join the vertex to the crossing point. It splits the angle into two equal halves.

example.q: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB = 6 cm. Where does it cut AB?
steps: Open the compass to more than 3 cm (say 4 cm)
Draw arcs above and below AB from A, then from B with the same opening
Join the two crossing points; it cuts AB at its midpoint M
example.answer: At M, where AM = MB = 3 cm, at a right angle

learn.reallife: Builders find the middle of a wall, and gardeners mark paths that stay equally far from two trees, using the perpendicular bisector idea.

games.title: Perpendicular bisector steps
items: Draw the line segment AB
Open the compass to more than half of AB
With centre A, draw arcs above and below AB
With the same opening and centre B, draw arcs cutting the first two
Join the two crossing points

games.title: Bisector truths
items: The perpendicular bisector of AB meets AB at 90°.
That is why it is called perpendicular.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B.
This is the special property of the perpendicular bisector.
For a perpendicular bisector, the compass opening can be less than half of AB.
Then the arcs from A and B would not meet.
An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal angles.
Bisect means cut into two equal parts.
Bisecting a 90° angle gives two 30° angles.
Half of 90° is 45°.
We need a protractor to draw a perpendicular bisector.
A ruler and a compass are enough.

quiz.q: AB = 8 cm. Its perpendicular bisector cuts AB at M. How long is AM?
quiz.explain: The perpendicular bisector cuts AB at its midpoint, so AM = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the bisector meets AB at the middle

quiz.q: What angle does the perpendicular bisector of AB make with AB?
quiz.explain: Perpendicular means it meets AB at a right angle, 90°.
steps: 'Perpendicular' means meeting at a right angle.
So the perpendicular bisector makes 90° with AB.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'bisector' (half) with the angle it makes

quiz.q: To draw the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment, what compass opening should you use?
quiz.explain: The opening must be more than half of 6 cm (3 cm), otherwise the arcs from the two ends will not meet.
steps: The arcs from A and B must meet above and below AB.
They meet only if the radius is more than half of AB.
So the compass opening must be more than 3 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any small opening works

quiz.q: An angle of 80° is bisected. What is each new angle?
quiz.explain: Bisecting cuts the angle into two equal parts: 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.
steps: Bisecting cuts an angle into two equal parts.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle instead of halving it

quiz.q: P is a point on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and PA = 5 cm. What is PB?
quiz.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A and B, so PB = PA = 5 cm.
steps: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B.
P is on it, so PB = PA.
quiz.mistake: Halves or doubles the distance

quiz.q: A 60° angle is bisected, and then one of the halves is bisected again. What is the smallest angle made?
quiz.mistake: Bisects only once

quiz.q: Which tools do you need to construct a perpendicular bisector?
options: A protractor and a set square
quiz.explain: The compass draws the arcs and the ruler joins the crossing points.
steps: The compass draws equal arcs from A and B.
The ruler joins the points where the arcs cross.
So you need a ruler and a compass.
Answer: A ruler and a compass
quiz.mistake: Thinks angles must be measured with a protractor

quiz.q: In an angle bisector construction, why are the two new angles equal?
options: The two triangles formed are congruent by SSS, so the matching angles are equal
quiz.explain: The arcs make two triangles with all three sides equal (SSS). Congruent triangles have equal matching angles.
steps: The arcs make two triangles whose three pairs of sides are equal.
So the triangles are congruent by SSS.
Matching angles of congruent triangles are equal.
So the two new angles are equal.
Answer: The two triangles formed are congruent by SSS, so the matching angles are equal
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the construction to congruent triangles

teach.ask: Gappu wants to find the exact middle of a stick drawn on paper, without a scale. How can he do it with a compass?
teach.praise: Wow! Two arcs from each end and one line — Gappu found the exact middle!
teach.nudge: How wide should the compass be, and what do you join at the end?

focus: Steps to construct a perpendicular bisector

Why the angle bisector works (congruent triangles by SSS)

It passes through the midpoint of AB at 90°
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B
traps: Don't use a compass opening of half of AB or less — it must be more than half.
Don't double the angle when bisecting — halve it.
Don't mix up 'bisector' (equal halves) with the 90° angle it makes.

topics.title: Perpendiculars at a point, from outside, and with ropes

learn.hook: More than 2,500 years ago, builders in India made perfect right angles with just a knotted rope!
points: 90° at a point P on a line: with centre P, draw an arc cutting the line at A and B (so PA = PB). Then draw arcs from A and B with a bigger radius; they cross at Q. PQ is perpendicular to the line.
It works because Q is equally far from A and B, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Perpendicular from an outside point Q: with centre Q, draw an arc cutting the line at A and B. From A and B draw equal arcs crossing at R on the other side. QR is perpendicular to the line.
The Sulba-Sutras, ancient Indian texts for building fire altars, used ropes. A rope knotted into 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 equal parts, pulled into a triangle, gives a right angle.
Other rope triangles such as 5, 12, 13 also give right angles.

example.q: Draw a perpendicular to line l from a point Q outside it.
steps: With centre Q, draw an arc cutting l at A and B
With centres A and B and the same radius, draw arcs crossing at R on the other side of l

learn.reallife: Masons still use a knotted string or a 3-4-5 check to make sure walls meet at a right angle.

games.title: Perpendicular at a point on a line
items: Mark point P on line l
With centre P, draw an arc cutting l at A and B
With a bigger radius, draw arcs from A and B that cross at Q
Join PQ — it is perpendicular to l

games.title: Ropes and arcs
items: A rope knotted into 3, 4 and 5 equal parts makes a right angle
3, 4, 5 is a right-triangle set.
The Sulba-Sutras were written for building fire altars
They give exact rules for altar shapes.
For a perpendicular from an outside point, the first arc is drawn with centre at that point
It cuts the line at two points.
A rope knotted into 2, 3 and 4 parts makes a right angle
2, 3, 4 does not give a right angle.
In the perpendicular-at-a-point method, PA must equal PB
P must be the midpoint of AB.

quiz.q: To construct a 90° angle at point P on a line, what is the first step?
options: Draw a line from P at any slant
With centre P, draw an arc cutting the line at two points A and B
quiz.explain: The arc makes PA = PB, so P becomes the midpoint of AB.
steps: We want P to be the midpoint of two points on the line.
With centre P, draw an arc cutting the line at A and B: PA = PB.
Then we can draw the perpendicular bisector of AB through P.
So the first step: arc with centre P cutting the line at A and B.
Answer: With centre P, draw an arc cutting the line at two points A and B
quiz.mistake: Reaches for a protractor instead of compass steps

quiz.q: In that construction, why is PQ perpendicular to the line?
options: Q is equally far from A and B, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB
Because Q is above the line
quiz.explain: Points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, which passes through the midpoint P.
steps: Arcs of equal radius from A and B meet at Q, so QA = QB.
Points equally far from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
P is the midpoint of AB, so PQ is that perpendicular bisector.
So PQ is perpendicular to the line.
Answer: Q is equally far from A and B, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason that does not use equal distances

quiz.q: To draw a perpendicular from a point Q outside a line, what is the first step?
options: With centre Q, draw an arc cutting the line at two points
Draw a line parallel to the given line
Draw a circle with centre on the line
quiz.explain: The two cutting points are equally far from Q; then we find another point equally far from them.
steps: With centre Q, draw an arc cutting the line at two points.
These two points are equally far from Q.
Then find another point equally far from both and join it to Q.
So the first step is the arc with centre Q cutting the line twice.
Answer: With centre Q, draw an arc cutting the line at two points
quiz.mistake: Starts the construction on the line instead of at Q

quiz.q: A rope is knotted into 12 equal parts to make a right angle. How are the parts shared among the three sides?
quiz.explain: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, and a 3-4-5 triangle has a right angle.
steps: A 3-4-5 triangle has a right angle.
So the parts are shared as 3, 4 and 5.
quiz.mistake: Splits the rope equally, which gives 60° angles

quiz.q: In a 3-4-5 rope triangle, each part is 50 cm. How long is the longest side?
quiz.explain: 5 parts × 50 cm = 250 cm.
steps: The longest side of a 3-4-5 triangle has 5 parts.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 4-part side

quiz.q: What were the Sulba-Sutras used for?
options: Building fire altars of exact shapes and sizes
quiz.explain: They gave geometric rules, including right angles made with ropes, for building altars.
steps: The Sulba-Sutras are ancient Indian texts with geometric rules.
They gave rope methods, like right angles, for exact shapes.
These were used for building fire altars.
So they were used for building fire altars of exact shapes and sizes.
Answer: Building fire altars of exact shapes and sizes
quiz.mistake: Does not know the purpose of these ancient texts

quiz.q: Which other knotted-rope triangle also gives a right angle?
steps: Test: smaller² + middle² = largest² means a right angle.
So 5, 12 and 13 parts give a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Picks lengths that just look close

quiz.q: How many equal parts are needed in total for a 5-12-13 rope triangle?
steps: Total parts = sum of the three sides.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two of the sides

teach.ask: Gappu has no protractor, only a compass and a ruler. How can Gappu make a right angle at a point on a line?
teach.praise: Right angle made! Gappu's corner is perfect.
teach.nudge: What should Gappu draw first, with the compass point on P?

revise.summary: A perpendicular can be constructed at a point on a line or from a point outside it using compass arcs. The ancient Sulba-Sutras used a rope knotted into 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts to make right angles.
focus: Constructing a 90° angle at a point on a line
Constructing a perpendicular from an outside point
Why the construction works (perpendicular bisector)
Rope triangles 3-4-5 and 5-12-13
remember: At P on a line: arc from P cuts the line at A and B; bigger arcs from A and B cross at Q; PQ ⊥ line
From outside Q: arc from Q cuts the line at A and B; equal arcs from A and B cross at R; QR ⊥ line
Sulba-Sutras: ancient Indian texts for building fire altars; 3, 4, 5 rope triangle gives a right angle
traps: Don't split a rope into equal sides — that gives 60° angles, not a right angle.
Don't start the outside-point construction on the line — start at Q.
Don't add only two sides when counting rope parts: 5-12-13 needs 30 parts.

topics.title: Copying an angle and drawing parallel lines

learn.hook: Copy any angle exactly — no protractor, no measuring — just a compass and a ruler!
points: To copy ∠ABC at point Q on a ray: with centre B draw an arc cutting the arms at D and E.
With the same radius and centre Q, draw an arc cutting the ray at R.
Open the compass to the distance DE. With centre R, cut the second arc at S. Join QS: ∠SQR = ∠ABC.
It works because triangles DBE and SQR have three equal sides, so they are congruent (SSS).
To draw a parallel through P: draw a transversal through P cutting line l, then copy the angle at l to P in the corresponding position.

example.q: Draw a line through P parallel to l without a protractor.
steps: Draw a line through P cutting l at Q
Copy the angle at Q to P, in the corresponding position
The new line makes equal corresponding angles, so it is parallel to l
example.answer: A line through P parallel to l

learn.reallife: Tailors copy the angle of a collar from one shirt to another with just a measuring tape and a marker — the same idea.

games.title: Copying an angle
items: With centre B, draw an arc cutting the arms of ∠B at D and E
With the same radius and centre Q, draw an arc cutting the ray at R
Open the compass to the distance DE
With centre R, cut the second arc at S
Join QS

games.title: Copy check
items: Copying an angle needs a protractor
Only a compass and ruler are needed.
The copy works because of SSS congruence
The two triangles have three equal sides.
The first two arcs must have the same radius
That makes two pairs of equal sides.
To draw a parallel, copy the angle in the corresponding position
Equal corresponding angles mean parallel lines.
Copying an angle anywhere always gives a parallel line
It must be in the corresponding (or alternate) position.

quiz.q: Which tools are needed to copy an angle exactly?
options: A ruler and a compass only
quiz.explain: Arcs of equal radius and one copied distance are enough.
steps: Copying an angle uses arcs of equal radius and one copied distance.
A compass draws arcs and copies distances; a ruler draws straight rays.
So a ruler and a compass only.
Answer: A ruler and a compass only
quiz.mistake: Thinks a protractor is always needed

quiz.q: What is the first step in copying ∠ABC?
options: With centre B, draw an arc cutting both arms
Draw a circle around the whole angle
quiz.explain: The arc from the vertex marks equal distances on both arms.
steps: First mark equal distances on both arms of ∠ABC.
With centre B, draw an arc cutting both arms (at D and E).
So the first step is an arc with centre B cutting both arms.
Answer: With centre B, draw an arc cutting both arms
quiz.mistake: Starts at the wrong point

quiz.q: After the first arc, what is drawn at the new point Q?
options: An arc with centre Q and the same radius
An arc with centre Q and a bigger radius
quiz.explain: Using the same radius makes QR equal to BD.
steps: At the new point Q, draw an arc with the same radius as before.
This makes QR = BD (and QS = BE).
So draw an arc with centre Q and the same radius.
Answer: An arc with centre Q and the same radius
quiz.mistake: Changes the compass opening

quiz.q: Which distance is copied with the compass in the third step?
options: The distance from B to Q
The distance DE between the points where the first arc cut the arms
quiz.explain: Copying DE gives the third pair of equal sides.
steps: After two equal-radius arcs, we need the third side.
Copy the distance DE between the points where the first arc cut the arms.
So the copied distance is DE.
Answer: The distance DE between the points where the first arc cut the arms
quiz.mistake: Copies an arm length instead

quiz.q: Why is the copied angle equal to the original?
options: The two triangles are congruent by SSS
quiz.explain: BD = QR, BE = QS and DE = RS, so the triangles are congruent and the matching angles are equal.
steps: BD = QR and BE = QS (same radius); DE = RS (copied).
Three pairs of equal sides → the triangles are congruent by SSS.
Matching angles of congruent triangles are equal.
So the copied angle equals the original.
Answer: The two triangles are congruent by SSS
quiz.mistake: Does not link the construction to congruence

quiz.q: To draw a line through P parallel to l, which angle do we copy?
options: The angle between l and itself
The angle a transversal makes with l, placed at P in the corresponding position
quiz.explain: Equal corresponding angles make the lines parallel.
steps: Draw a transversal through P cutting l.
Copy the angle it makes with l at P, in the corresponding position.
Equal corresponding angles make the lines parallel.
So copy the transversal's angle with l at P, corresponding position.
Answer: The angle a transversal makes with l, placed at P in the corresponding position
quiz.mistake: Copies the angle in the wrong position

quiz.q: A transversal makes 72° with l. What angle must be copied at P, in the corresponding position, for a parallel line?
quiz.explain: Corresponding angles must be equal: 72°.
steps: Rule: for parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
quiz.mistake: Uses the linear-pair angle

quiz.q: Suppose you copy the 72° angle at P in the alternate position instead. Is the new line still parallel to l?
options: Yes — equal alternate angles also give parallel lines
quiz.explain: Equal alternate angles also show that two lines are parallel.
steps: Equal alternate angles also show that two lines are parallel.
Copying 72° in the alternate position gives equal alternate angles.
So Yes — the line is still parallel to l.
Answer: Yes — equal alternate angles also give parallel lines
quiz.mistake: Thinks only one angle rule proves lines parallel

teach.ask: Gappu wants to copy a 50° angle but lost the protractor. Teach Gappu the compass trick!
teach.praise: Copied perfectly! Gappu's angle matches exactly.
teach.nudge: Which two distances must Gappu keep the same?

revise.summary: An angle can be copied with only a ruler and compass, and the copy is equal because the two triangles are congruent by SSS. Copying a corresponding angle lets us draw a parallel line.

learn.hook: Why are bathroom tiles squares and beehive cells hexagons — but never pentagons? Let's crack the tiling code!
points: A tiling covers a flat surface with shapes that leave no gaps and do not overlap.
At every point where corners meet, the angles must add up to 360°.
Only three regular polygons tile on their own: equilateral triangles (6 × 60°), squares (4 × 90°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°).
A regular pentagon has 108° angles. 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so pentagons leave gaps.
Different shapes can tile together: two regular octagons (135° each) and one square (90°) fit around a point.

learn.hook: Remove two opposite corners from a chessboard. Can 31 dominoes cover the rest? Colours give a surprising answer!
points: A tangram is a square cut into 7 pieces: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, 1 square and 1 parallelogram.
If the whole square has area 16 units, each large triangle is 4, the medium triangle 2, each small triangle 1, the square 2 and the parallelogram 2.
A 2 × 1 domino always covers 2 squares, so a region with an odd number of squares (like 5 × 5 = 25) can never be tiled by dominoes.
Colouring argument: on a chessboard each domino covers one black and one white square.
Removing two opposite corners (both the same colour) leaves 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other, so no domino tiling exists — even though 62 is even.

steps: 15 is odd, so some square is always left over

learn.hook: An equation is like a see-saw in perfect balance. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — and it stays balanced!

Use the opposite operation to undo: undo + 4 by subtracting 4; undo × 3 by dividing by 3.
For two-step equations, undo the adding or subtracting first, then the multiplying or dividing.

topics.title: Mind the mistake, mend the mistake

learn.hook: Even toppers make mistakes — the champions are the ones who spot and fix them!
points: Sign error: in 2x + 5 = 13, subtracting 5 gives 2x = 8, not 2x = 18.
Unlike terms: 3x + 4 cannot become 7x — a number and an x-term can't be joined.
Wrong division: 5x = 20 gives x = 20 ÷ 5 = 4, not 100 or 15.
Brackets: 3(x + 2) = 21 means 3x + 6 = 21, not 3x + 2 = 21.
To mend a solution, redo the wrong step and then check by putting the answer back into the original equation.

learn.hook: Centuries ago, Indian mathematicians wrote 'yā' for the unknown — long before anyone used x!
points: Bījagaṇita is the Indian name for algebra; Bhāskara II (Bhāskarāchārya) wrote a famous book with this name around 1150 CE.
Āryabhaṭa (5th century), Brahmagupta (7th century) and Bhāskara II solved equations. Al-Khwārizmī (9th century, Baghdad) wrote 'al-jabr', which gave us the word algebra.
Old Indian notation: 'yā' for the unknown, 'kā' for a second unknown, 'rū' for a known number, and a dot over a number to show it is negative.
Brahmagupta's rule: for Ax + B = Cx + D, x = (D − B) ÷ (A − C).
A problem from the Bakhshali manuscript: B gets 2 times A, C gets 3 times B and D gets 4 times C. Together they get 132. So A = x, B = 2x, C = 6x, D = 24x, 33x = 132 and x = 4.

learn.hook: Think of any number. Double it, add 10, halve it, subtract your number... you got 5, didn't you?
points: Trick: think of n → double: 2n → add 10: 2n + 10 → halve: n + 5 → subtract n: 5. Always 5!
Letter-numbers explain the magic: the n disappears at the end, so every starting number gives the same answer.
Make your own trick: '× 3, + 12, ÷ 3, − the number' always gives 4.
Heads and feet: 20 heads and 56 feet, children (2 feet) and donkeys (4 feet). If donkeys = d, children = 20 − d.
2(20 − d) + 4d = 56 → 40 + 2d = 56 → d = 8 donkeys and 12 children. Two unknowns became one!

example.q: 20 heads and 56 feet belong to children and donkeys. How many of each?
steps: Let donkeys = d, so children = 20 − d

quiz.q: Think of n. Double it and add 10, then halve the result. Which expression do you have now?
quiz.mistake: Halves only the 2n and not the 10

quiz.q: In the same trick, you now subtract the number you first thought of. What is the result if you started with 7?
quiz.explain: (2 × 7 + 10) ÷ 2 − 7 = 12 − 7 = 5. It is 5 for every starting number.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve the 10

quiz.q: Trick: think of a number, multiply by 4, add 20, divide by 4, subtract the number. What is the result?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer depends on the starting number

quiz.q: Which trick always ends with 3?
quiz.explain: (2n + 6) ÷ 2 − n = n + 3 − n = 3. The others give 1.5, n + 6 and 1.
quiz.mistake: Does not test the trick with a letter-number

quiz.q: Children and donkeys have 20 heads and 56 feet in all. How many donkeys are there?
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of children

quiz.q: With 20 heads and 56 feet (8 donkeys), how many children are there?
steps: Heads = 20 (each child and donkey has 1 head); donkeys = 8.
quiz.mistake: Divides the feet by 2

quiz.q: There are 30 heads and 84 feet (children and donkeys). With d donkeys, which equation fits?
quiz.explain: Children = 30 − d with 2 feet each; donkeys = d with 4 feet each.
steps: Donkeys = d, so children = 30 − d (30 heads).
Feet: children 2 each → 2(30 − d); donkeys 4 each → 4d.
quiz.mistake: Uses one letter for both groups

quiz.q: Solve 2(30 − d) + 4d = 84 to find the number of donkeys.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 2d = 24
